A.note: Monochrome beige ruin field with a visible tile grid on the ground. Rubble is low-poly blobs and plank sticks. The ruined walls are thin extruded slabs. The tiny troop cluster at the bottom is lost in the frame. There is no smoke, fire or ships, so the bombardment reads as debris scattered on a flat plane. Intact buildings are clean, saturated boxes next to the sand-coloured ruin, which looks inconsistent.

B.note: Nearly the same as A. The ruin walls are slightly taller and more tangled, and the troop group is a bit denser. It still has the grid-textured ground, blob rubble, no smoke and a lost focal point. The ruins merge into a beige mush that is slightly less legible than A.

C.note: The best frame. It has a real sense of place: sea, sky, hills, a citadel on the ridge, a bell tower, garden plots and a bastioned sea wall. The dense town carpet of terracotta roofs gives scale and depth. Weaknesses: identical box buildings with repeated roofs and chimney cubes, a visible ground grid, tiny troops, no smoke or ships, and no sign of bombardment, so it doesn't match the 'partly in ruins' brief. The Mediterranean look is plausible for the period but generic.

why: C is the only frame with environmental context, depth, sky and a dense, readable town, while A and B are near-identical beige ruin fields with grid-textured ground, blob rubble and a barely visible troop group.
top_fix_for_best: Break up the repeated box-and-roof pattern with varied building heights, footprints and roof types. Remove the visible ground tile grid with a proper textured street and earth material. Then add narrative: smoke columns, damaged buildings and a few ships in the harbour, plus larger troops or civilians in the foreground for scale. A lower, closer camera with depth-of-field and atmospheric haze would sell it as cinematic.
